verdict: OK to lend in Bahadurgarh plastics and rubber, but only to converters with verified fire compliance and clean waste handling; avoid polybag and pouch units and any borrower burning scrap on site.
title: Bahadurgarh Plastics & Rubber Processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Bahadurgarh plastics unit buys polymer granules or scrap, runs it through extruders, moulders or film lines, and sells film, pouches, moulded parts or reprocessed granules to nearby packers, traders and OEMs.** Cash turns on the spread between resin cost and conversion price, so the real levers are machine utilisation, power and burner fuel, and how fast the buyer pays. Rubber reprocessing works the same way, with reclaim volumes and export buyers setting the pace. **Ask for the unit's monthly resin purchase register and power bill before anything else; if the two do not move together, stop and ask why.**

## Where value and cash actually sit
**Value sits in the conversion margin, not the resin, and that margin is thin and easily eaten by fuel and freight.** The working-capital cycle is short but unforgiving: granules are bought on advance or short credit while film and pouch buyers pay late, so the gap is funded by the bank. Capex is modest per line but continuous, and a single fire can wipe out a year of profit. **So when a proposal lands, check the fire NOC and the insurance cover on stock and plant; if either is missing or lapsed, ask for it before sanction.**

## What has changed now
**The local picture is mixed and the local sources are thin, so lean on first principles and peers.** Polybag and pouch production in the Jhajjar-Bahadurgarh belt has fallen 50%, forcing owners to fit diesel burners [2] — that is a cost and compliance problem at the same time. The Tribune reports burning of plastic waste and metal drums continuing in the Bahadurgarh industrial belt despite round-the-clock surveillance [1], and four factories in Modern Industrial Area were gutted in a fire in December 2025 [3]. Against that, Haryana GST collections are up 10.1% Apr-to-date versus India's 6.1% [D], and all-India plastics output (NIC 22) is up 21.4% YoY [D]. **Treat the state GST number as a demand signal, not a licence to lend to every unit in the belt.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue rigid moulders, pipe and profile makers, and reprocessors selling to industrial buyers, and avoid polybag and pouch units until their output recovers.** Peer results support the industrial side: Supreme Industries grew sales tonnage 19% YoY with operating profit up 45% [6], Apcotex posted revenue up 44% YoY in H1 [7], and GRP's rubber recycling revenue rose 34% [4]. **Take monthly stock and book-debt statements plus power bills; if stock cover falls below the sanctioned limit for two months running, cut the limit.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for diesel burner fuel bills rising while output stays flat, which means the unit is buying compliance instead of selling product.** Watch for scrap burning on site or waste leaving without manifests — a booking under [1] shuts a unit fast. Watch for insurance lapses and any repeat fire incident [3]. **If a borrower's GST turnover drops for two consecutive quarters while its bank limit stays drawn, freeze fresh disbursement and inspect the godown.**
